Subject: Post-call: SLO/Performance qualification — streaming + throughput targets

Hi Sara / Tom —

Thanks again for the time today — good to get alignment on the end-to-end use case and initial SLO targets. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can loop in engineering: 

Recap from the call:
- Use case: assistant for clinician notes + quick follow-ups via chat (streaming desirable for UX).
- Desired SLOs you mentioned:
  * Streaming: P95 latency target ~200ms (per-token?), aiming for interactive feel
  * Non-streaming (batch responses): P95 <= 300ms for short replies
  * Concurrency: baseline ~30 concurrent sessions, peak ~80 concurrent sessions
  * Throughput: expected steady-state ~150 req/min, peaks up to ~600 req/min during shift changes
- Model family: you plan to start with an open LLM (70B family) but are open to smaller/quantized variants to meet cost/latency needs.

Attachments: I’m attaching a short SLO template and our Redwood perf playbook to capture requirements and common levers.

Immediate asks / next steps:
1) Can you confirm the latency targets above (are the streaming numbers per-token or end-to-end first-byte?) — please reply inline so we capture exact SLOs.
2) I’ll loop in our SE/infra folks to propose concrete configuration options and ballpark unit economics.
3) If helpful, we can schedule a technical deep-dive (30–45m) this week to review live traces and sizing.

Cc’ing Vivek and Dev to pick this up on the sizing/cost side. Vivek, Dev — please see Sara/Tom’s notes and advise on levers we should propose (batching, caching, quantization, model variants, streaming endpoint configs) and rough cost guidance for: baseline (30 concurrency) and peak (80 concurrency / 600 req/min).

Thanks —

— Priyom

Subject: Re: Post-call: SLO/Performance qualification — streaming + throughput targets

Thanks Priyom — quick clarifications from our side: 

- Streaming numbers: when I said ~200ms I meant time-to-first-token (startup latency) for the streaming endpoint; we expect per-token additions to be small (~10–20ms).
- For non-streaming endpoints, P95 <= 250ms is actually what we'd like for short assistant responses (under ~300 tokens).
- Concurrency: baseline is 30 active clinicians; peak 80 concurrent active sessions is what we see during morning handoffs.
- Throughput: your note about 150 req/min baseline aligns; peaks could hit 500–700 req/min for short bursts (not sustained).
- Model: we are currently evaluating a 70B open checkpoint, but we are absolutely open to a 13B or 30B variant if it materially reduces cost and meets SLOs. 

Key question for Redwood: which cost/performance levers would you recommend to hit the streaming startup + P95 goals at the lowest cost? Specifically: continuous batching, KV/prefix caching, model quantization profiles (4-bit vs 8-bit), and model variant suggestions. Also please include any constraints for concurrency per GPU and expected token-level cost ranges so our finance team can ballpark monthly spend.

If possible, please include a short example config for: 1) low-latency streaming for 200ms startup at ~50 concurrency, and 2) cost-optimized non-streaming config for bulk generation.

— Sara

Subject: RE: Fwd: Post-call: SLO/Performance qualification — streaming + throughput targets

Thanks — summary + recommended levers below. I’ve kept things high-level for the customer; we can convert into a one-pager for Sara/Tom.

Quick summary of constraints from Sara: TTF (streaming) ~200ms, P95 non-streaming <=250ms, baseline 30 concurrency (target config for 50), peaks ~80 concurrency, burst throughput up to ~600 req/min. Open to model variants.

Recommended levers (cost vs latency):
1) Low-latency streaming endpoint (primary)
   - Use dedicated low-latency serving pools (single-tenant / reserved instances) for strict startup targets — reduces cold-start jitter.
   - Continuous batching with small max batch latency (e.g., 5–10ms) to preserve throughput while keeping per-request latency low. Redwood supports continuous batching with configurable max batch latency.
   - Model variant: prefer a quantized 30B (q4f or int8) for best balance; 70B will increase time-to-first-token unless heavily sharded — costs increase significantly. 13B can meet TTF but may have degraded accuracy for clinical prompts.
   - KV / prefix caching: definitely use prefix caching for system prompts and frequent context (saves compute and reduces latency for warmed sessions). Cache common clinician prompt templates in memory (KV cache) — this reduces per-request compute for repeated interactions.
   - Networking: colocate inference in the same region as your application tier and use streaming over HTTP/2 or SSE to minimize added network latency.

2) Cost-optimized non-streaming (bulk)
   - Use higher-batch-size endpoints with lazy/async batching for bulk generation (increase max batch latency to 50–100ms), or switch to cheaper model variant (13B quantized) for bulk workflows.
   - Use autoscaling policies that prioritize throughput: scale based on queue length and token/sec rather than low concurrency thresholds.

3) Quantization/profile guidance
   - Q4f (4-bit fine-tuned aware quant) is often the sweet spot for 30B models — near FP16 quality with 2–3x cost reduction.
   - Int8 works well for many 70B variants but needs kernel & runtime tuning; expect higher memory footprint than q4f for same model quality.

4) Concurrency per GPU / sizing
   - For a 30B q4f optimized runtime on A100-class hardware (or equivalent), expect ~8–12 streaming concurrents per GPU with low startup targets if using continuous batching and prefix caching. So for 50 concurrency target, plan for ~5–8 GPUs in a dedicated pool depending on traffic burstiness and desired safety margin.
   - For bulk/off-peak generation, a single GPU can handle higher batched throughput (dozens of requests/sec) using larger batch sizes.

5) Ballpark costs (very rough)
   - Low-latency 30B q4f dedicated pool to support ~50 concurrent streaming sessions: estimate $X–Yk/month (we should convert to tokens/hour once we validate average tokens per request).
   - Cost-optimized 13B quantized for bulk: ~30–50% lower compute cost vs 30B.
   - We’ll produce a token-level cost estimate once Sara confirms average tokens per session and monthly active clinicians.

Suggested next steps
- Technical deep-dive (30–45m) with Sara/Tom, Vivek (SE), and Dev (infra): we’ll present two config options (low-latency streaming 30B-q4f and cost-optimized 13B-quant) with expected GPU counts and ballpark monthly compute.
- Sara/Tom to confirm average tokens per session (median and 95th) and expected monthly active clinicians — that will let us translate sizing into $/month.

I’ll assemble a short one-page comparison and sample configs (runtime flags, batch settings, cache settings) after the deep-dive.

— Dev Patel
